extracted.intended_audience: interactive fiction authors, designers, and enthusiasts (especially those interested in choice-based/CYOA works)
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive and historical overview of choice-based (CYOA) interactive fiction, including its formal structure, presentation patterns, authoring tools, and cultural/legal/contextual considerations for authors and designers. Useful for people building or studying branching/hyperlinked narrative games.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice-based IF structural definition (story nodes + choices/hyperlinks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice-based IF (also called choose your own adventure or CYOA) refers to a style of interactive fiction where the game is assembled from a set of story nodes and related choices or hyperlinks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A typical play move is moving from one story node to another; the game is composed of these nodes and the choices connecting them. This is the fundamental structural requirement of the form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical turn format (passage plus choices/hyperlinks)
rubrics_metrics.description: A typical turn in CYOA will consist of a passage of text describing the current situation of the game. In some works, this is followed by a short list of explicit options to choose from; in other works, hyperlinks are scattered throughout the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design each turn as a readable descriptive passage that presents the player's situation and then offers clear choice points, whether as an explicit option list or as inline hyperlinks that lead to new sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branching and multiple endings determined by player choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Each book/game offered multiple endings, where the outcome depended upon what the reader wanted to happen next in the linear narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice-based IF typically implements branching paths that lead to different endings; authors should plan branching structure and endings so they meaningfully reflect player choices (example: CYOA page-turn choices that send readers to numbered pages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stateless branching vs depth/complexity (statefulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The simple, stateless branching narrative trees of the Choose Your Own Adventure gamebooks do not represent the depth and complexity of many games authored with modern choice IF systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid equating all choice IF with simple, stateless trees; modern systems may include variables, persistent state, complex conditions, and nonlinear structure that provide greater depth. Labeling complex work as 'CYOA' can be misleading or derisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of choices: explicit option lists vs inline hyperlinks
rubrics_metrics.description: Some works present a short list of explicit options to choose from; in other works, hyperlinks are scattered throughout the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a presentation style that fits tone, readability, and UX: explicit lists make choices obvious (good for younger readers), while inline hyperlinks can create a more fluid reading experience or embed choices in prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoring tools and supported platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Authoring tools for choice-based IF include Twine, Squiffy, Undum, ChoiceScript, and ink, among others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select an authoring system appropriate to your design goals (e.g., Twine for accessibility and rapid hypertext, ChoiceScript for stat-based choice games, ink for narrative scripting). More authoring systems are listed on the IFWiki authoring systems page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and format conventions (young-reader, page-per-turn CYOA books)
rubrics_metrics.description: From about 1981 to about 1995, Bantam published the Choose Your Own Adventure series of gamebooks for young readers (ages 9-12), in which the story was told a page at a time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing for a particular audience (e.g., children), follow appropriate conventions for length, complexity, and presentation (short passages, clear explicit choices, page-per-turn pacing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark/legal labeling caution ('choose your own adventure' term)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2019, ChooseCo, the rightsholders of the original CYOA series, issued takedown notices to authors on itch.io who had marked their own games as 'choose your own adventure' or 'CYOA'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about labeling or marketing your work with trademarked terms; consider alternative descriptors (e.g., 'choice-based interactive fiction') to avoid legal issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility and diversity enabled by tooling (the Twine revolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the early 2010s, the release of Twine opened up IF development to a huge number of creators. Many of these were people from marginalised groups, including the LGBTQ+ community, who found in Twine a means to express their own stories and feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use accessible, low-barrier tools to broaden participation and enable diverse voices; tooling choices shape who can author and what kinds of stories get told (examples: Anna Anthropy, Porpentine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial viability and critical/narrative excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: A number of commercial developers such as Choice of Games and inkle began producing choice-based IF for profit. In 2014, Inkle's 80 Days achieved commercial success and critical acclaim, winning awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choices and narrative depth with commercial/audience expectations in mind if seeking broader market success; narrative quality, polish, and production values can lead to awards and wider recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural and interface variations (CYOA variations and hybrids)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many CYOA variations and hybrids (educational CYOA, graphic-novel adaptations, CYO-RPG, hybrid interfaces) and discussions/articles (e.g., 'CYOA structures' series and 'Not All Choice Interfaces Are Alike').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore hybrid forms and alternative interfaces (educational uses, graphic formats, RPG integrations); the choice-based form is adaptable and can be combined with other genres and mechanics depending on design goals.
